stimulus.description: A long straight cylindrical wire of radius $R=2\text{ mm}$ carries a current along its axis. The current density depends on the distance $r$ from the axis as $J(r)=J_0r/R$, where $J_0=2\times10^{5}\text{ A/m}^{2}$. Use $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the diagram of the cross-section of the wire (shown as a circle, with the current out of the page), draw a circular Amperian loop of radius $r<R$ and draw an arrow showing the direction of the magnetic field on the loop.
parts.model_answer: A circle concentric with the wire inside its boundary, with the field arrow tangent to the circle and pointing counterclockwise for a current out of the page.

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws a circular loop concentric with the wire and inside its boundary ($r<R$)
required_elements: concentric loop of radius r < R
common_errors: draws the loop off-center or outside the wire

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws the field arrow tangent to the loop (perpendicular to the radius)
common_errors: draws a radial arrow

rubric_rows.criterion: Gives the correct sense, counterclockwise for a current out of the page, by the right-hand rule
common_errors: draws a clockwise arrow

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the magnitude of the magnetic field at a distance $r<R$ from the axis in terms of $\mu_0$, $J_0$, $R$ and $r$.
parts.model_answer: $I_{enc}=\int_0^rJ_0\dfrac{r'}{R}2\pi r'\,dr'=\dfrac{2\pi J_0r^3}{3R}$ and Ampère's law $B\,2\pi r=\mu_0I_{enc}$ gives $B=\dfrac{\mu_0J_0r^2}{3R}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the current in a thin ring, $dI=J\,2\pi r'\,dr'$
common_errors: uses $J\pi r'^2$ without integrating

rubric_rows.criterion: Integrates from $0$ to $r$ to obtain $I_{enc}=2\pi J_0r^3/(3R)$
common_errors: integrates to $r^2$ instead of $r^3$

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies Ampère's law to obtain $B=\mu_0J_0r^2/(3R)$
common_errors: uses $B=\mu_0I_{enc}/r$ without $2\pi$

parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic field at $r=1.5\text{ mm}$.
parts.model_answer: $B=\mu_0J_0r^2/(3R)\approx94.2\,\mu\text{T}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains about 94.2 with units of microteslas (accept any value within 2 percent)

notes: A student measures the resistance $R$ of pieces of the same resistance wire, of diameter $d=0.5\text{ mm}$, for several lengths $L$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe an experimental procedure to collect the data for the resistance as a function of the length. Include the equipment and the measurements, how the length is changed, and one way to reduce the uncertainty in the resistance.
parts.model_answer: Stretch a single wire straight along a meterstick, connect it in a circuit with a battery and an ammeter, measure the potential difference across the section of length $L$ with a voltmeter and the current with the ammeter, change the length by moving the contact, and compute $R=V/I$; keep the same wire and temperature, and reduce the uncertainty by using small currents (to limit heating) or by repeating and averaging.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies how the resistance is found (voltmeter across the section and ammeter in series, $R=V/I$, or an ohmmeter) and how the length is measured
common_errors: measures the length without a way to get the resistance

rubric_rows.criterion: Changes only the length while keeping the same wire (diameter and material) and the temperature the same
required_elements: change only the length, same wire and temperature

rubric_rows.criterion: Reduces the uncertainty by using small currents to avoid heating, or by repeating the measurement and averaging, or by using a longer range of lengths (any one earns the point)
required_elements: small currents or repeat and average or longer range (any one earns the point)

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: For a uniform wire $R=\rho L/A$. Identify the quantities that should be plotted on the vertical and horizontal axes so that the data produce a straight line whose slope can be used to determine the resistivity $\rho$.
parts.model_answer: Plot $R$ on the vertical axis against $L$ on the horizontal axis; the slope is $\rho/A$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies $R$ (vertical) versus $L$ (horizontal), with slope $\rho/A$
common_errors: plots R versus 1/L

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: On a blank grid whose scale you choose, plot the data in the form identified in part B and draw a best-fit line. Label the axes with quantities and units and use a scale that fills most of the grid.

rubric_rows.criterion: Axes are labeled with quantities and units and the scale fills most of the grid
common_errors: scale uses less than half the grid

rubric_rows.criterion: Plots the five points $(L,R)$ accurately
Draws a straight best-fit line through the trend of the points
common_errors: connects the dots

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Use the best-fit line to determine the resistivity of the wire material. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: The slope is $\rho/A\approx5.16\,\Omega/\text{m}$ with $A=\pi(d/2)^2=0.1963\text{ mm}^2$, so $\rho=\text{slope}\cdot A\approx1.01e-06\,\Omega\cdot\text{m}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the slope of the best-fit line using two points on the line (about 5.16 ohms per meter; accept any value within 5 percent)
common_errors: uses data points rather than points on the line

rubric_rows.criterion: Relates the slope to $\rho$: $\rho=\text{slope}\cdot A$ with $A=\pi d^2/4$ and the diameter converted to meters
common_errors: uses the diameter as the radius in the area

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $\rho$ of about 1.01e-06 with units of ohm-meters (accept any value consistent with the student's own slope from D1)
alt_solutions: a value of rho consistent with the student's own slope from D1

ap_physics_c_electricity_and_magnetism-f.title: Field of a charged spherical shell

stimulus.description: A thin spherical shell of radius $R=10\text{ cm}$ carries a charge $Q=4\text{ nC}$ spread uniformly over its surface. The shell is nonconducting and in vacuum. Use $k=9.0\times10^{9}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^{2}/\text{C}^{2}$.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: A student claims that the electric field at the center of the shell is the same as the electric field just outside its surface. Do you agree or disagree with the claim? Justify your answer using Gauss's law.
parts.model_answer: Disagree. For a spherical Gaussian surface inside the shell no charge is enclosed, so by symmetry and Gauss's law the field there is zero, while just outside the field is $kQ/R^2$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Disagrees with the claim
common_errors: agrees because the field is continuous

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that a spherical Gaussian surface inside the shell encloses no charge, so the field inside is zero
common_errors: says the field is zero because the charges cancel pairwise without using Gauss's law

rubric_rows.criterion: Contrasts this with a surface just outside, which encloses the whole charge $Q$ and gives a nonzero field $kQ/R^2$
common_errors: says the outside field is also zero

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the magnitude of the electric field at a distance $r>R$ from the center and calculate its value at $r=R$ (just outside the surface).
parts.model_answer: $E\,4\pi r^2=Q/\varepsilon_0$ gives $E=kQ/r^2$; at $r=R$ it is $\approx3600\text{ N/C}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies Gauss's law with a concentric spherical surface: $E\,4\pi r^2=Q/\varepsilon_0$

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains $E=kQ/r^2$

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the field at $r=R$ of about 3600 with units of newtons per coulomb (accept any value within 2 percent)

parts.model_answer: The field falls to one quarter (about $900\text{ N/C}$), because outside the shell $E\propto1/r^2$.

common_errors: states that the field is halved

ap_physics_c_electricity_and_magnetism-f.title: Energy balance while charging a capacitor

stimulus.description: A battery of emf $\varepsilon=12\text{ V}$ and negligible internal resistance charges an initially uncharged capacitor of capacitance $C=50\,\mu\text{F}$ through a resistor. The capacitor ends fully charged.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: A student claims that all of the energy supplied by the battery during the charging is stored in the capacitor. Do you agree or disagree with the claim? Justify your answer by comparing the work done by the battery with the energy stored.
parts.model_answer: Disagree. The battery does work $q\varepsilon=C\varepsilon^2$ on the charge it moves, but the capacitor stores only $\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$; the other half is dissipated as thermal energy in the resistor.

rubric_rows.criterion: Disagrees with the claim
common_errors: agrees that the energy is conserved in the capacitor

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies by identifying the work done by the battery as $Q\varepsilon=C\varepsilon^2$
common_errors: uses $\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$ for the battery's work

rubric_rows.criterion: Compares with the energy stored, $\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$, and concludes that the remainder is dissipated in the resistor
common_errors: says the remainder is stored in the wires

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive expressions for the work done by the battery, the energy stored in the capacitor, and the thermal energy dissipated in the resistor, and calculate the thermal energy for the given values.
parts.model_answer: $W_{battery}=C\varepsilon^2$, $U=\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$ and $Q_{thermal}=W_{battery}-U=\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2\approx3600\,\mu\text{J}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the battery's work as $W=q\varepsilon$ with $q=C\varepsilon$, giving $C\varepsilon^2$
common_errors: writes $W=\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes the stored energy $U=\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$ and the thermal energy $Q=W-U=\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$
common_errors: states that the thermal energy depends on $R$

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the thermal energy of about 3600 with units of microjoules (accept any value within 2 percent)

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: The experiment is repeated with a resistor of twice the resistance. Predict whether the thermal energy dissipated in the resistor increases, decreases or stays the same, and justify your prediction.
parts.model_answer: The thermal energy stays the same, because the total energy dissipated is $\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$ regardless of $R$; a larger $R$ only makes the charging slower.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the thermal energy stays the same
common_errors: states that the thermal energy doubles because $P=I^2R$

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with the energy balance: the dissipated energy equals $W-U=\tfrac12C\varepsilon^2$, which does not depend on $R$
required_elements: Q = 1/2 C epsilon^2 independent of R
common_errors: argues only that the current is smaller with a larger resistor
